extracted.intended_audience: citizens/voters considering ratification of the U.S. Constitution; policymakers and legislators
extracted.subtask_description: Argumentative guidance and interpretive principles about the proper scope, limits, and interpretation of federal taxation and related constitutional clauses (necessary & proper, supremacy), directed to citizens evaluating the proposed Constitution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Powers commensurate with objects
rubrics_metrics.description: A government ought to contain in itself every power requisite to the full accomplishment of the objects committed to its care, and to the complete execution of the trusts for which it is responsible; every power ought to be commensurate with its object.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Principle framed as a first principle: where an authority is entrusted with certain ends, it must possess the necessary faculties to achieve them. Anti-pattern: denying powers needed for the entrusted ends (leaving government unable to perform its duties).

rubrics_metrics.name: Means proportioned to the end
rubrics_metrics.description: The means ought to be proportioned to the end; the ability to do a thing presupposes the power to employ the means necessary to its execution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this as a test when construing grants of power: if an end is conferred, laws necessary to effect that end are legitimate. Example: a tax power implies power to pass laws necessary and proper to collect taxes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unlimited power to provide for national exigencies
rubrics_metrics.description: As the duties of superintending the national defense and of securing the public peace involve a provision for casualties and dangers to which no possible limits can be assigned, the power of making that provision ought to know no other bounds than the exigencies of the nation and the resources of the community.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constitutional design should permit broad capacity to meet unforeseeable future contingencies (especially defense). Anti-pattern: constraining government to present exigencies only, which risks incapacity in future emergencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revenue is essential engine — taxation power implied
rubrics_metrics.description: As revenue is the essential engine by which the means of answering the national exigencies must be procured, the power of procuring that article in its full extent must necessarily be comprehended in that of providing for those exigencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing the scope of fiscal powers, treat taxation authority as essential and integral to other constitutional duties (defense, peace). Practical implication: taxation authority must be sufficiently broad to fund national obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal taxation needed because state-level collection is unavailing
rubrics_metrics.description: Theory and practice prove that the power of procuring revenue is unavailing when exercised over the States in their collective capacities; the federal government must of necessity be invested with an unqualified power of taxation in the ordinary modes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Justifies central taxation authority on practical grounds: states acting collectively cannot reliably supply national needs. Anti-pattern: relying on states' voluntary compliance to fund national obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Security against usurpation depends on structure, not limiting powers
rubrics_metrics.description: All observations founded upon the danger of usurpation ought to be referred to the composition and structure of the government, not to the nature or extent of its powers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If one fears federal usurpation, address institutional checks and composition (dependence on the people), rather than curtail textual grants of power; imagination about usurpation leads to irresolution and poor reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: States retain powers unless explicitly divested
rubrics_metrics.description: The State governments would retain all the rights of sovereignty which they before had, and which were not, by that act, exclusively delegated to the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret grants to the Union narrowly in the sense that states keep residuary authorities unless the Constitution explicitly (or necessarily by repugnancy) divests them. Example: the Constitution inserts negative prohibitions where it was intended to take away state powers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusive delegation arises in three cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Exclusive delegation (alienation of State sovereignty) exists only (1) where Constitution expressly grants exclusive authority to the Union; (2) where it grants authority to the Union and prohibits the States from exercising like authority; (3) where a state exercise would be absolutely and totally contradictory and repugnant to the Union's authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this threefold rule to test whether a federal grant excludes state authority. Examples from text: exclusive legislation over the federal district (case 1); power over duties on imports/exports plus prohibition on states (case 2); uniform rule of naturalization (case 3).

rubrics_metrics.name: Concurrent taxation authority for most taxes
rubrics_metrics.description: The power of imposing taxes on all articles other than exports and imports is manifestly a concurrent and coequal authority in the United States and in the individual States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret the Constitution to allow both federal and state taxation concurrently except where exclusivity is explicit. Anti-pattern: assuming federal grant of taxation necessarily excludes state taxation absent explicit language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negative pregnant interpretation — prohibitory clause implies affirmation elsewhere
rubrics_metrics.description: The restriction on States laying duties on imports and exports amounts to a 'negative pregnant' — a negation of one thing and an affirmance of another (i.e., affirming state authority to tax other articles).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use prohibitory clauses as evidence of the framers' intention to leave other powers with the States. Avoid sophistry that would read a prohibitory clause as implying state powers exist only 'subject to the control' of the national legislature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repugnancy must be immediate constitutional contradiction to extinguish state power
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not a mere possibility of inconvenience but an immediate constitutional repugnancy that can by implication alienate and extinguish a pre-existing right of sovereignty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When deciding whether a federal law implicitly excludes state authority, require actual constitutional repugnancy (direct contradiction) rather than speculative policy conflict or inconvenience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessary and Proper clause is declaratory, not expansive
rubrics_metrics.description: The clause authorizing Congress 'to make all laws which shall be NECESSARY and PROPER for carrying into execution the powers vested' is largely declaratory: it declares that a power to do an end includes authority to enact the necessary means.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the Necessary and Proper clause as stating what necessarily follows from vesting powers, used as a caution against cavilling refinements. Anti-pattern: construing the clause as a standalone sweeping new power divorced from the specific grants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supremacy limited to laws made pursuant to the Constitution
rubrics_metrics.description: The Constitution and laws made in pursuance thereof, and treaties made by authority, shall be the supreme law of the land — expressly confined to laws made pursuant to the Constitution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not treat every act of the Union as automatically supreme; only acts within constitutional authority are supreme. Acts beyond granted powers are usurpations and not protected by supremacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who judges necessity/propriety: government first, people ultimately
rubrics_metrics.description: The national government must judge, in the first instance, of the proper exercise of its powers, and its constituents (the people) in the last; if the federal government overpasses bounds, the people must appeal to the standard they have formed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical rule of political accountability: allow government initial discretion while reserving ultimate redress and judgment to the citizenry and constitutional mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constitutions should provide capacity for remote futurity
rubrics_metrics.description: Constitutions of civil government are not to be framed upon a calculation of existing exigencies, but upon a combination of these with the probable exigencies of ages; there ought to be a capacity to provide for future contingencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design constitutional powers to be broad enough to meet unforeseeable future needs (especially defense and commerce). Anti-pattern: framing constitutions narrowly based only on immediate present needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mutual forbearance and concert to avoid practical inconveniences
rubrics_metrics.description: Though overlapping taxation might produce inconveniences (e.g., accumulation of taxes on same object), mutual interest should dictate a concert which avoids material inconvenience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy expectation: federal and state authorities will coordinate or forbear in practice to prevent destructive duplicative taxation. Use political prudence rather than constitutional fiction to resolve such tensions.

rubrics_metrics.name: State revenue needs largely limited compared to federal defense costs
rubrics_metrics.description: The objects requiring federal provision (e.g., defense, wars, national debts) are unlimited and will absorb the greater share of national expense; state expenditures (domestic police, legislature, encouragement of agriculture/manufactures) are comparatively moderate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical justification for granting broad federal taxation: most heavy public expenditures will be national (war, debt, navy), so states will retain adequate means for their more limited needs.
